prompt: A service promises 99.9% availability, measured over a 30-day month. How many minutes may it be down in that month?
hint: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes; take the 0.1% that is left over.

prompt: The stock check passes through the Portal B2B (99.9%), the service bus (99.5%) and SAP ECC (99.0%), and all three must be up. What is the availability of the chain, in per cent, to two decimal places?
hint: In series, multiply the three availabilities.

prompt: Two independent copies of a component are each 99.5% available, and either one can do the work alone. On paper, what is the availability of the pair, in per cent?
hint: The pair is down only when both are down: 1 − (1 − a)².

prompt: A proposal says a second bus node will take the bus from 99.5% to 99.9975%. Rui's outage record shows that 18 of last year's 43.8 hours came from an expired certificate and a faulty deployment. What is wrong with the proposal?
hint: Ask what each of those two causes would have done to the second node.

choices.text: A second node doubles the number of parts that can fail, so the pair is below 99.5%
choices.why: The pair still survives every failure that hits one node alone; it is better than one node, only by less than the formula says.

choices.text: The formula assumes independent failures, and both causes would hit both nodes
choices.why: Right: a shared certificate and a shared deployment are common-mode failures, so about 18 hours remain and the pair reaches about 99.79%.

choices.text: The 18 hours were planned work, which availability figures leave out
choices.why: An expired certificate and a broken deployment are unplanned outages, and the measured 99.5% includes them.

choices.text: The formula holds for a passive standby, not for two active nodes
choices.why: Active or passive, the formula rests on independence; the arrangement changes the failover time, not the shared causes.

prompt: Match each term to what it is for the Portal B2B.
hint: A measurement, a target, a contract, and what the target leaves over.

pairs.right: the share of submissions confirmed within 5 seconds
99.5% of submissions over a rolling 30 days
a contract saying what happens when the target is missed
the 120 failed submissions the target allows in 30 days

right_distractors: the four hours a week the service may be stopped for maintenance

prompt: Rota's route-planning service answers about 40,000 valid requests in 30 days, against an objective of 99.8%. How many failed requests does its error budget allow in those 30 days?
hint: The budget is 1 minus the objective, times the valid events.

prompt: One Saturday night the load balancer in front of the portal refused connections for an hour. The SLI computed from the portal's own application log shows 100% for that night. Why?
hint: Think about which requests can leave a line in that log.

choices.text: A request refused before reaching the portal leaves no line in its log
choices.why: Right: a service measured from its own logs cannot see what never reached it, which is why Joana measures at the load balancer and with an outside probe.

choices.text: Refused connections are not valid events, so the SLI leaves them out of the count
choices.why: "Valid" excludes what was never the system's to get right, like an order over the credit limit; a bakery that could not connect is exactly the failure the SLI is for.

choices.text: Saturday night is inside a planned window
choices.why: The portal has no Saturday window in the lesson, and a window would not make a refused connection disappear from a well-placed measurement.

choices.text: The SLI is a ratio over 30 days, and one lost hour simply rounds away to 100%
choices.why: Failed requests in that hour would still lower the ratio; the problem is that they were never counted at all.

prompt: The EDI provider's contract promises 99.5% a month and a credit of 10% of the R$ 6,000 fee below that. Orders worth about R$ 4 million a day arrive through it. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: Compare what the contract pays with what the business loses.

choices.text: Ask for a higher percentage, since 99.5% is below what Serra Alta needs
choices.why: A higher number with the same remedy still pays a fraction of a fee; the business need is met by design, not by a better clause.

choices.text: The credit covers the risk, as long as somebody claims it in time
choices.why: R$ 600 against a day of orders worth millions covers nothing; the credit is a refund of part of a fee.

choices.text: The SLA is a price term; the gap is covered by design
choices.why: Right: the vendor's SLA says what it refunds, and the difference between that and what the business needs is design work: a queue, a second route, a manual fallback.

choices.text: An SLA measured at the vendor's edge is invalid and should be renegotiated
choices.why: Measuring at its own edge is how vendors write these contracts; it is a fact to design around, not a defect that makes the contract void.

prompt: Rota's database is 99.5% available outside its planned window, and it is stopped on purpose every Saturday from 23:00 to 01:00. Counted around the clock, what is its availability in per cent, to two decimal places?
hint: A week has 168 hours; multiply by the share of the week outside the window.

prompt: Coleta's file loads on Sundays only because somebody once moved the Sunday run of the SAP job to 06:00, and the rule exists only in the job scheduler. What does the lesson say should change?
hint: Designed for the window, or surprised by it?

choices.text: Move SAP's window to a weekday night, when fewer bakeries order
choices.why: That moves the collision rather than recording it; Coleta sends a file every night of the week.

choices.text: Write SAP's window and the Sunday timing into the interface contract
choices.why: Right: a rule that both teams depend on belongs where both read it, not in one scheduler that the next tidy-up will change without knowing.

choices.text: Leave it: the rule works, and when a job runs is the receiver's business
choices.why: It works until somebody tidies the schedule; a timing both sides rely on is part of the contract.

choices.text: Send the collections through the bus synchronously, so a failure shows at once
choices.why: A synchronous call into a system that is down on purpose fails every Sunday; the file waiting in its directory is the right shape.

prompt: SAP's window is Sunday 01:00 to 05:00. Suppose Rui moves the bus's window to Sunday 03:00 to 07:00 instead. How many hours of planned downtime a week does the stock check, which needs both, then have?
hint: A chain's planned downtime is the union of its members' windows.

prompt: SAP's loader checks the length of every line of Coleta's fixed-width file. Which of these changes to the file are breaking? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether each existing reader keeps working without changing anything.

choices.text: Adding a new field at the end of each line
choices.why: Breaking: every line becomes longer than the loader accepts.

choices.text: Writing the file at 01:00 instead of 01:30
choices.why: Compatible: it still arrives before the 02:00 load, and nothing the reader relies on has moved.

choices.text: Widening the litres field from 9 to 11 digits
choices.why: Breaking: in a fixed-width record every field after it moves.

choices.text: Sending kilograms in the field that used to hold litres
choices.why: Breaking, and silently: every line still loads, with the wrong quantity.

prompt: A new version of Coleta starts writing the date the file was loaded where it used to write the date of collection. The format, the lengths and the control totals are unchanged. What happens?
hint: Which part of the contract changed?

choices.text: Every line loads, and Saturday's milk is recorded as Sunday's
choices.why: Right: a change of semantics passes every check that looks at the shape, which is why the contract states what each field means.

choices.text: The loader rejects the file, because the dates no longer match the header
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's contract compares each line's date with the header, and the lengths and totals still agree.

choices.text: The control totals catch it, since the totals cover each field
choices.why: The totals count records and add litres; the dates are not in them, and the litres have not changed.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since a date is a date
choices.why: The day decides which day's milk a farm is paid for; the same format with a different meaning is a breaking change.

prompt: The portal team wants consumer-driven contract tests, with Pact, for the portal's use of Salesforce's API. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: Who would have to run the tests before releasing?

choices.text: It works the same as with Rota, since any API with a schema can take consumer tests
choices.why: Consumer-driven contracts need the producer to run the consumers' tests in its build, and Salesforce will not run Serra Alta's.

choices.text: It is pointless with a vendor, since a vendor never breaks its interfaces
choices.why: Vendors do change interfaces with releases; the lesson keeps tests against their sandbox precisely to find that.

choices.text: Keep the tests, and run them against the vendor's sandbox before each upgrade
choices.why: Right: the vendor will not run them, so Serra Alta runs its own tests of what it relies on before the upgrade reaches production.

choices.text: Ask Salesforce to sign the Pact file as part of the contract
choices.why: A vendor selling one platform to many customers does not adopt each customer's tests; the lesson's answer is on Serra Alta's side.

prompt: A consumer that reads only the fields it needs and lets unknown ones pass is, in Martin Fowler's name for it, a ___ reader.
hint: It puts up with what it does not recognise.

prompt: Put the steps of a degraded-mode runbook in the lesson's order.
hint: From noticing the failure to closing the mode.
items: Detect that the dependency is down
A named person declares the degraded mode
Drain what accumulated once the dependency is back
trap: Telling people before the fallback is on promises something not yet working, and reconciling before the backlog has drained checks a moving target.

prompt: SAP is unavailable for 3 hours while the portal accepts orders for later confirmation at 150 an hour. When SAP returns, the job creating them handles 450 an hour while new orders keep arriving at 150. How many hours does the backlog take to clear?
hint: First the backlog, then how fast it shrinks.

prompt: On Sunday night the portal shows bakeries a stock figure taken before SAP's window. What does the lesson say makes that honest?
hint: What would the bakery need to know to judge the figure?

choices.text: Refreshing it from a copy of SAP's tables during the window
choices.why: A replica follows SAP and is down with it, which is why lesson 1 rejected reading SAP's tables at all.

choices.text: Subtracting a safety margin from every product before showing it
choices.why: A margin hides the uncertainty instead of stating it, and the bakery still cannot tell how old the figure is.

choices.text: Blocking orders until SAP confirms the stock is there
choices.why: That is the error page the degraded mode exists to avoid; the portal accepts and confirms later.

choices.text: Showing the time the figure was taken
choices.why: Right: the age is what makes stale data honest; the same figure without its time is a lie that happens to be nearly right.

prompt: At 22:00 the state tax authority stops answering, and the yoghurt trucks are due to leave the Juiz de Fora plant at 04:00. By the lesson, what must already be true for them to leave on time?
hint: Who switches the mode on, and what must the software already do?

choices.text: A queue in front of the authority that holds the invoices until it answers again, so they are kept safe
choices.why: Store and forward holds the invoices, and the trucks with them: goods that cannot be invoiced cannot be shipped.

choices.text: Paper invoices
choices.why: The lesson describes contingency modes defined by the NF-e rules, issued and later regularised, not a return to paper invoices.

choices.text: A named person entitled to switch to contingency, and issuing software set up for it beforehand
choices.why: Right: the mode is the issuer's to switch on, and the software must support it before the night it is needed.

choices.text: A second provider of authorisation contracted by Serra Alta
choices.why: Authorisation comes from the tax authorities and the contingency arrangements their rules define, not from a provider Serra Alta hires.

prompt: Log backups are taken every 20 minutes, and in the busiest hour about 180 sales orders arrive. In the worst case, how many orders can a failure in that hour lose?
hint: The worst failure comes just before the next backup.

prompt: Recovering a system takes 30 minutes to detect, 30 minutes to decide, a restore of 1,800 GB at 600 GB an hour, 1 hour of logs and 1.5 hours of checks. How many hours does the recovery take?
hint: The restore is one of five steps.

prompt: A document system backs up its database at 01:00 and its content files at 04:00, and is restored from both. Which documents does the restore get wrong?
hint: Documentum had the opposite order. Work out what each backup contains.

choices.text: Documents stored between 23:00 and 02:00, as at Serra Alta
choices.why: Those were the hours of Documentum's two backups; the gap here is between 01:00 and 04:00, and runs the other way.

choices.text: Documents stored from 01:00 to 04:00: their files return with no record
choices.why: Right: the files were saved at 04:00 and the records at 01:00, so files from between are restored with nothing pointing at them.

choices.text: None: each backup succeeded
choices.why: Each backup succeeding is exactly what hid the Documentum gap; two moments restore to a state that never existed.

choices.text: Documents stored from 01:00 to 04:00: their records return with no file
choices.why: That is the Documentum case, where the database was the newer copy; here the files are newer than the records.

prompt: The stock-check chain is 98.41% available outside SAP's planned window. Counted around the clock, with SAP also down every Sunday from 01:00 to 05:00, what is it in per cent, to two decimal places?
hint: Multiply by the share of a 168-hour week that is outside the window.

prompt: Regina gives Joana one change to make the bakery's basket more available. Which one moves the number most?
hint: Look at where the hours are, and at which factor a change can remove.

choices.text: A second bus node, which the formula says takes the bus to 99.9975%
choices.why: With the shared causes it takes the bus to about 99.79%, which moves the chain by about three tenths of a point while SAP's 1% stays.

choices.text: Raising the portal's own availability from 99.9% to 99.99%
choices.why: The portal is 0.1% of the 1.6%; perfecting it leaves the chain at 98.505%.

choices.text: Lowering the portal's objective to 98%, so that the chain it depends on can meet it
choices.why: That changes the promise, not the basket; the bakeries are just as unable to order.

choices.text: Serve the cached figure with its time when SAP is silent, and confirm later
choices.why: Right: it takes SAP, the largest factor and its Sunday window, out of the path while the bakery waits.

prompt: Joana writes the registry entry for the portal's call to SAP's available-to-promise service. Which of these belong in it? Choose all that apply.
hint: A contract states what the consumer relies on, including timing and failure.

choices.text: SAP's window, Sunday 01:00 to 05:00
choices.why: Yes: the receiver states its window so that the caller does not discover it.

choices.text: What the portal does when the call times out
choices.why: Yes: error behaviour is one of the seven parts, and here it is the cached figure with its time.

choices.text: The number of nodes the bus runs on
choices.why: That is how Rui meets his objective, not something the portal relies on; the objective goes in, the mechanism stays with its owner.

choices.text: The owners on both sides
choices.why: Yes: an entry names who answers for the producer and for the consumer.

prompt: SAP is restored to a point 15 minutes before it failed. In those 15 minutes the bus had delivered EDI orders and the chains had their acknowledgements. What does the lesson say must happen before the restore is over?
hint: The restored system went back in time; its neighbours did not.

choices.text: Nothing more: a 15-minute RPO means those orders were accepted as lost
choices.why: The RPO bounds what the database may lose; the chains still believe they ordered, so somebody has to replay or re-enter those orders.

choices.text: Replay from the bus's message store into consumers that are safe against duplicates, then reconcile
choices.why: Right: the integration's RPO depends on resending, and a replay from 15 minutes before resends some messages that did arrive.

choices.text: Restore the bus to the same point, so that the two agree
choices.why: Rolling the bus back too loses the messages that could rebuild SAP's missing work, and the chains still hold their acknowledgements.

choices.text: Ask the chains to send their orders again
choices.why: Some partners can resend and some cannot; the lesson starts from the copy Serra Alta controls, the bus's message store.
